By Charity L. Cohen / 10/06/2026 Alumni , College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences
EAST GREENSBORO, N.C. (Oct. 6, 2026) – Forever a North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University Aggie and now a Hillman College Falcon, former Mister A&T Joshua Suiter ‘22 is starring in the Netflix reboot of the 1980s and 1990s hit sitcom “A Different World.”
The series, which debuted at No. 1 on Netflix in the U.S., has already been renewed for a second season. It builds on the cultural impact of the original series, which helped shape national perceptions of historically Black college and university (HBCU) life and inspired generations of students.
Following a new generation of students at the iconic fictional HBCU, Hillman College, the sequel explores the lives of today’s students while examining the legacy of those who came before them. The series’ writing team includes Ashley Laverne Jackson, daughter of late civil rights leader the Rev. Jesse Jackson ‘64.
Suiter portrays Andre, a fellow Hillman student alongside Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), daughter of original characters Whitley (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne (Kadeem Hardison). As Deborah begins her journey at Hillman, she works to establish her own identity beyond her parents’ legacy while experiencing the highs and challenges of campus life.
“Seeing all the love for Andre really hit home,” Suiter said. “He’s one of my favorite characters thus far, and we created him from scratch, so to know that the hard work is being received and folks want more encourages me to keep going.”
Suiter discovered his calling for acting and musical theater at 7, quickly realizing that hours spent studying lines and practicing techniques felt like minutes. That passion led him to N.C. A&T, where he earned a B.F.A. in professional theatre from the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences.
While at A&T, Suiter built a strong foundation in the performing arts, gaining experience both on stage and behind the scenes. One of his notable performances was in “Ain’t Misbehavin’” during the university’s first Town & Gown Gala in 2019, where he first met Guy, who reprises her role as Whitley in the reboot.
In addition to acting, Suiter worked as a theater technician and developed skills in the marketing and business aspects of performance and the entertainment industry. This versatility helped propel him into his professional career.
“I came in as a creative, but what A&T did between Alpha Phi Alpha, the classes, talking business with professors and serving as Mister A&T sharpened me on the business side,” said Suiter. “It sharpened my networking skills while showing me how to be authentic to who I am.”
As a talented and emerging actor who most recently appeared in the Hulu series “All’s Fair,” performing alongside prominent Hollywood actors, starring in “A Different World” represents a full-circle moment for Suiter as an HBCU alumnus, bringing him into a reimagined version of a series he grew up watching.
“When you talk about an HBCU experience, I’m putting mine up there with the best of them,” he said. “I have so many experiences to pull from with the run of this show, with the character Andre. Hillman even has a heartbeat of its own, so it’s been fun exploring what that feels like as a student there, while still carrying that Aggie Pride in my heart.”

By Davide Dionisi and Kielce Gussie
On the evening of October 5, the United Nations spokesperson Farhan Haq announced the latest tragedy in Sudan while speaking to journalists: âAn airstrike in South Kordofan targeting two trucks belonging to the World Food Programme (WFP) killed a driver and damaged food supplies. In a second incident, a child was killed and twelve others were injured: five boys and seven girls.â
In a statement , the WFP stressed that the two trucks were clearly marked and the attack comes just one day after another WFP truck hit an explosive device after delivering food aid in Dilling.
Furthermore, the statement explained how these attacks show âthe increasingly challenging security environment in Sudan and the risks that aid workers face when delivering life-saving assistance to communities in need.â Despite the risks, the UN organization stressed its commitment to providing support and aid to those in need.
In 2025, the UN aid coordination office OCHA reported more than 30 million people are in need of humantiarian assistance.
The Sudanese army has been fighting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since April 2023, following disagreements between the two sides over issues such as the integration of their respective forces as part of the transition towards civilian government. Last month, the US State Department said that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces nor the RSF, nor their respective leaders, ârepresent a legitimate and constitutional government for Sudan.â
The conflict has forced more than 14 million people to flee their homes and has triggered waves of ethnically motivated killings. According to the United Nations, more than seven million people, particularly in Darfur, are living in conditions of food insecurity.
After months of deadlock, the US is seeking to revive diplomatic efforts to find a solution to the conflict.
âWe reaffirm the United Statesâ steadfast commitment, together with our Egyptian partners and other regional and international allies, to promoting a political solution to the crisis,â said Massad Boulos, the US Senior Adviser for Arab and African Affairs, in a post on X. He said he had attended a luncheon hosted by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, head of the Sudanese army.
The Egyptian president stressed that âEgypt will continue to make every possible effort, at the regional and international levels, to promote a political solution to the crisis, help bring the war to an end, and alleviate the humanitarian suffering of the Sudanese people.â He added that this âwill enable Sudan to restore security and stability and embark on reconstruction.â
President Al-Sisi also reaffirmed to General Burhan his countryâs âunwavering supportâ for the âbrotherly Sudanese peopleâ and its commitment to preserving Sudanâs unity, sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national institutions, including the regular army.
The meeting in Egypt came less than two weeks after Washington denied the Sudanese army chief a visa to attend a planned address to the United Nations General Assembly. According to Sudanese sources, the move was reportedly linked to a US-backed ceasefire proposal, which Khartoum has so far resisted.

articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is the largest in decades in the U.S.
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is the largest in decades in the U.S.
articles.content_orig:
The state has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, health officials said Monday, making it the largest outbreak in the U.S. in more than three decades.
NEW YORK (AP) — Pennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials said Monday, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades.
The U.S. is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 reported cases, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The nation has seen eight reported measles-associated deaths in the past two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Since the beginning of last year, large outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest with 997 cases reported.
The governor of New York on Monday declared a disaster emergency because of measles cases in neighboring states and in rural areas of New York. The executive order extends the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and allows nurses to join doctors in ordering testing. The state has more than 100 cases this year.
Health officials say Pennsylvania’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia. There have been 1,004 cases, including 198 hospitalizations and five deaths , state officials said.
Health experts attribute such outbreaks to low vaccination rates.
It’s been decades since a U.S. state has seen an outbreak surpass 1,000 cases, stretching back to a multiyear outbreak in New York City in the early 1990s that infected more than 4,500 people.
The nation eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks.
In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status .
Measles is highly contagious. It spreads when people who have it breathe, cough or sneeze, and through contaminated surfaces. It can also linger in the air for two hours. Up to 9 out of 10 people who are susceptible will get the virus if exposed, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
U.S. measles infections have been surging in recent years, as fewer kids get routine vaccines due to parental waivers, healthcare access issues and rampant disinformation.
Pennsylvania and New York are not the only states with a growing problem. Another is Ohio, with more than 200 cases this year. Like in Pennsylvania, some of the hardest-hit Ohio counties have significant Amish populations, which tend to have lower vaccination rates.
Meanwhile, CDC officials have quietly begun to acknowledge measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania.
State officials in August announced that two unvaccinated residents died after being infected with measles.
The announcement quickly came under fire as a clash erupted between vaccine-promoting Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a Trump administration appointee with a history of raising alarms about established vaccines.
Since then, Pennsylvania has reported three additional deaths.
But for weeks, the CDC — which Kennedy oversees — did not count any deaths on its measles data dashboard, instead saying it was seeking more information. That changed two weeks ago, when one death was finally counted, and again last week when a second was added to the agency’s tally.

articles.title_orig: Russia’s neighbor backs push to lift ban on nuclear weapons, prompting outcry from Moscow
articles.title_zh: Russia’s neighbor backs push to lift ban on nuclear weapons, prompting outcry from Moscow
articles.content_orig:
The Kremlin on Tuesday warned a preliminary decision by Lithuanian lawmakers to lift a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear weapons and the potential deployment of a NATO military base in the country will mark "another significant escalation" of regional tensions.
The comments come shortly after Lithuania's parliament voted in favor of advancing a constitutional change on deploying nuclear weapons on its territory. It is the first of two ballots required for the change, with the latter scheduled for Jan. 12 next year.
The country, which is a member of both the European Union and NATO and shares a border with Russia's Kaliningrad exclave on the Baltic Sea, has been looking to remove the constitutional ban to strengthen its resilience amid growing security concerns.
Lithuania has been one of Ukraine's staunchest allies during Russian President Vladimir Putin 's more than 4½-year conflict with Kyiv, providing extensive military equipment and financial support.
President Donald Trump , meanwhile, said he would consider Lithuania's request for a permanent U.S. military base in the country. "They are friends of mine. They are great people, so we will certainly look at it," Trump said Monday.
Asked about the developments, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that they "cannot be perceived as anything other than a step toward escalating tensions, just as the deployment of nuclear weapons in a neighboring country cannot," according to Russian state news agency Tass.
"Neither of these developments will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent. On the contrary, they will, to our regret, mark yet another significant escalation of tensions. As for Russia, of course, Moscow will be forced to take all necessary measures to guarantee its own security," Peskov said.
Article 137 of Lithuania's constitution explicitly prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction and the establishment of foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory. The proposed amendment, which will require the support of at least 94 of the 141 members of parliament to pass, would remove that provision.
Lithuanian Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said scrapping the restriction would bolster the country's resilience and remove a legal distinction between Lithuania and other EU and NATO countries.
"We will ensure stronger support that could be available to us," Olekas said, according to state broadcaster LRT .
"By addressing the legal exceptions that Lithuania had compared with other EU and NATO countries, they will be gone and we will be equal," he added.

articles.title_orig: World-expanding stories from Pitt’s Nationality and Heritage Rooms
articles.title_zh: World-expanding stories from Pitt’s Nationality and Heritage Rooms
articles.content_orig:
From the latest big breakthrough to the most influential and inspiring figures on campus to Pitt in the community, Pittwire is your official source for what’s happening now.
Kati Csoman was still an undergraduate at the University of Pittsburgh when she lived in Hungary for the first time.
She spent the summer of 1988 in the rural northeastern village where her father had grown up. She slept in cousins’ homes, some of which didn’t have indoor plumbing. She picked up Hungarian with a village accent and, for the first time in her life, the language she heard at her childhood kitchen table became something she could speak back.
The immersion into this experience came courtesy of a Nationality Rooms scholarship .
“It really helped me to connect to that part of my life, which is so deeply a part of me,” she says. Three years later, she arrived back in Budapest on a state department fellowship to the U.S. embassy, watching firsthand how Hungary would remake itself after her father’s country voted in its first free elections since the 1940s.
“But, also, it totally changed my academic trajectory and then changed my professional trajectory, too.”
The scholarship launched Csoman (A&S ’89, SPIA ’96G) on a career in international education and connected her not only to her family’s history but also to a broader appreciation of ethnic communities and cross-cultural experiences.
And, eventually, it would lead her back to where it all began.
Today, Csoman is director of Pitt’s Nationality Rooms and Intercultural Exchange Programs, home to 31 spaces inside the Cathedral of Learning that represent the cultural heritages of many of Pittsburgh’s international communities.
The rooms were first imagined in the mid-1920s by Chancellor John Bowman, who wanted a celebration of Pittsburgh’s multicultural presence at the heart of his planned Cathedral of Learning . He turned to Ruth Crawford Mitchell, a Pitt sociologist already closely associated with the city’s ethnic communities through her work with second-generation immigrant students. She gave the program its shape at a time when nearly half of Pittsburgh residents were either born abroad or the children of immigrants. Communities could sponsor classrooms in the Cathedral and, once room construction was complete, leftover funds supported scholarships to send Pitt students abroad year after year. [Watch: Pitt's Nationality and Heritage Rooms are also celebrating a centennial this year. ]
Mitchell stepped back from the directorship in 1957. Shepherd Witman, who arrived at Pitt the following year to direct the Office of Cultural and Educational Exchange, oversaw the rooms during a transitional period, while E. Maxine Bruhns would take the reins in 1965. Bruhns led the Nationality Rooms for the next 55 years, when 12 of the 31 rooms were dedicated and scholarship programs were expanded significantly. Bruhns retired in 2020, with Csoman succeeding her the following year.
But the rooms touched Csoman’s own family long before. Her maternal grandfather had given a dime to help build the Cathedral. Csoman’s father later served on the Hungarian Room Committee, and Csoman herself volunteered with it before becoming the program’s director.
Since the late 1940s, the Nationality Rooms program has supported more than 1,800 Pitt undergrads or graduate students with study abroad scholarships, awarding nearly $5 million in funding. Thirty committees, plus the Women’s International Club, still meet; they fundraise and produce intercultural programming for the campus and wider community, and nearly all of the rooms presently serve as active classrooms or gathering places.
From conceptualization to fundraising to dedication, Pittsburgh’s international communities have shaped each of the rooms into a cultural self-portrait. Every room is designed with precise choices about what best represents a community and how it wants to be seen. A century in, the following stories, centered on the Chinese (dedicated 1939) , Italian (1949) , African Heritage (1989) and Philippine (2019) rooms, reveal examples of how these spaces bridge past and present and often reshape a life’s trajectory.
The Chinese community was not on Mitchell’s original list. In her earliest report to Bowman, Mitchell named 14 ethnic groups interested in building rooms; most were Eastern, Central or Southern European.
While the Chinese community was kept small in the United States by the Immigration Act of 1924 and other federal policies, a group of Chinese graduate students at Pitt sought out Bowman anyway. The Chancellor told them that if they could fundraise and form a committee, they could have a room, says Michael Walter, current manager of education programs for the Nationality Rooms. They organized quickly.
City-wide development also had a significant impact on Pittsburgh’s Chinese community at that time.
The city’s Chinatown neighborhood spanned multiple blocks downtown, but ended up physically divided in the 1920s and 1930s by construction of the city’s Boulevard of the Allies. Pittsburgh’s Chinatown district was all but gone in the following decades with residents moving outward.
Still, the Chinese Room became one of the first nine rooms at Pitt to reach completion. The German, Russian, Scottish, Swedish and Early American rooms were dedicated in 1938, while the Chinese, Czechoslovak, Hungarian and Yugoslav rooms came next in 1939.
The Chinese Room was modeled on an 18th-century reception hall in Beijing’s Forbidden City, the imperial palace at the heart of Ming and Qing dynasty rule.
This art installation inside Hillman Library examines a century of Nationality Rooms history. The installation will run through July 2027.
Yuefang Chang, a research associate professor in Pitt’s School of Medicine’s Department of Neurological Surgery, has been involved with the room for more than a decade, chairing the Chinese Room Committee for the past year and a half.
Chang has worked to learn the room’s history herself, noting that “even within the Chinese community, if they didn’t get a chance to go to the University, they just don’t know about its existence here.”
The first time Chang walked into the room, it surprised her. She had expected the colors to look brighter; instead, the dragons and phoenixes had softened over the decades.
But age and history are essential parts of the experience. Each Nationality Room’s design draws on cultural and traditional markers from before 1787 — the year of Pitt’s founding — meaning every room depicts something far older than the present. Decades of classes, holiday open houses and committee gatherings have only deepened that. Time is the point.
The Chinese Room is full of imperial signifiers: a five-clawed dragon on the ceiling (only the imperial dragon has five, a marker of leadership), phoenixes among peony blossoms, Confucius on the east wall and a round table at the center.
Chang’s committee today includes connections to Taiwan, Hong Kong, mainland China, Indonesia and the broader diaspora. This year, the Chinese Room committee and the John H. Tsui Memorial Scholarship, named for and seeded by a former chair, together will send seven students to China, Taiwan and Hong Kong.
“We all have different backgrounds,” Chang says. “I just hope this room will bring everybody together.”
On the steps of Florence’s Basilica of Santa Maria Novella, Lina Insana (A&S ’91, ’95G) sits with her students and reads from Giovanni Boccaccio’s “The Decameron,” which opens with 10 young Florentines gathered on those same steps in 1348, fleeing the Black Death.
“It was a wonderful way to read that together in a classroom that wasn’t a classroom at all,” she says. Insana, an associate professor of Italian in the Kenneth P. Dietrich School of Arts and Sciences, has taken students to Italy numerous times. She also knows what a Nationality Rooms scholarship makes possible.

Invest 92L is expected to strengthen into at least Tropical Storm Isaias in the Gulf this week. FOX Weather Hurricane Specialist Bryan Norcross breaks down all the possible scenarios and identifies which parts of the Gulf Coast could see the biggest impacts from this system.
A tropical depression is likely to form in the southern Gulf this week amid the quietest start to an Atlantic hurricane season since 1966, the start of the satellite era, with no hurricanes having formed this year.
THE LATEST FROM FOX WEATHER HURRICANE SPECIALIST BRYAN NORCROSS
The National Hurricane Center (NHC) has designated a brewing tropical disturbance as Invest 92L, and is giving the system high odds of becoming at least a tropical depression over the next two days. From there, how strong this storm becomes and exactly where it tracks still remains an open question.
WHAT IS AN INVEST DURING HURRICANE SEASON?
The term "invest" is used every hurricane season in the Atlantic and the Eastern and Central Pacific basins, accompanied by a number from 90 to 99 and either the suffix "L," "E" or "C," respectively.
Currently, a massive cold front is draped over Central Florida and is extending across the Gulf, bringing days of heavy rain to the Sunshine State through the workweek.
A storm could develop at the tail end of this front sometime on Thursday or Friday, potentially developing a more defined center that forecasters can track.
CALIFORNIA DECLARES STATE OF EMERGENCY AS POTENTIALLY HISTORIC SUPER EL NIÑO LOOMS
However, Wednesday will be a crucial day in determining this system's future as it begins to interact with more hostile El Niño-driven winds as well as dry air, which have helped suppress the hurricane season in the Atlantic overall.
"A more defined system in the southern Gulf will be able to defend itself from the hostile conditions," the FOX Forecast Center said.
"Some models now are hinting at possibly our first hurricane of the season, but there is still a lot to fine tune as uncertainty remains extremely high."
CENTURIES-OLD LAVA ROCK ARCH IN HAWAI'I VOLCANOES NATIONAL PARK COLLAPSES INTO OCEAN FOLLOWING HURRICANE NOLO
The FOX Forecast Center said the system could also struggle to develop or remain closer to the coast of Mexico .
Regardless of tropical development, forecasts show another round of heavy rain headed to parts of the Florida and Louisiana coasts by the weekend.
NOAA's Weather Prediction Center (WPC) has issued a Level 2 out of 4 flash flood risk for parts of the Southeast on Friday and Saturday.
Meanwhile, Gulf water temperatures are currently at their warmest levels on record dating back to 1982. Warm waters are conducive for tropical development.
September ended without a hurricane for the first time in 32 years, despite it being the climatological peak of the season.

A neighborhood destroyed in the aftermath of Hurricane Ian in Fort Myers, Florida.
(RICARDO ARDUENGO/AFP / Getty Images)
If the entire 2026 Atlantic hurricane season ends without a hurricane, it would mark the first hurricane-free Atlantic season of the modern era.

articles.title_orig: Chapel Intern gains global finance experience at World Bank Treasury
articles.title_zh: Chapel Intern gains global finance experience at World Bank Treasury
articles.content_orig:
Daniel Garcia Calao spent the summer gaining experience in global finance through a rotational internship with World Bank Treasury in Washington, D.C. Credit: Provided . All Rights Reserved .
UNIVERSITY PARK, Pa. — When Daniel Garcia Calao came to Penn State from Bogotá, Colombia, he hoped earning a college degree in the United States would open new opportunities. Four years later, his Penn State journey has taken him from Penn State Abington to Penn State University Park and, most recently, to Washington, D.C., for a summer internship with World Bank Treasury.
Garcia Calao, who is dual majoring in economics and finance with a minor in supply chain and information systems , spent the summer completing a rotational internship with World Bank Treasury . There, he worked with three teams, gaining experience in pensions, asset and liability operations, and advisory services.
“It was a truly global experience that strengthened both my technical skill set and my understanding of international financial institutions,” Garcia Calao said.
As a Chapel Executive Intern , Garcia Calao received enrichment funding through the Liberal Arts Career Enrichment Network to help cover his housing expenses in Washington. He also enrolled in LA 495 Undergraduate Field Experience, a half-credit course designed to help students reflect on and make the most of their internship experiences.
“The Chapel Executive Internship made the summer possible,” Garcia Calao said. “The funding covered my summer housing, which allowed me to save and invest my money and work toward my financial future.”
Garcia Calao was born and raised in Colombia and began his Penn State experience at the Abington campus. As an international student adjusting to a new environment, he found community through campus involvement, eventually serving as president of the Latine Student Organization and participating in student government and Lion Ambassadors .
After two years, he transitioned to the University Park campus, where he continued building his network and pursuing leadership opportunities.
Garcia Calao’s interest in economics and finance continued to grow as he progressed through Penn State. He added economics as a second major to broaden his knowledge and strengthen his preparation for internships and a career in finance. Courses in microeconomics, statistics and environmental economics gave him experience with concepts that he later encountered at World Bank Treasury, including central banking, economic policy and how different economies operate.
Daniel Garcia Calao explored Washington, D.C., while living and working in the city as a Chapel Executive Intern during summer 2026. Credit: Provided . All Rights Reserved .
Networking also played a major role in helping Garcia Calao find his internship. His path to the World Bank began after attending a Penn State Global Careers Institute event where a Penn State alumnus who worked at the World Bank spoke.
Garcia Calao reached out to the alumnus after the event to learn more, and that conversation helped introduce him to an organization where he had never pictured himself working.
“The whole reason I applied to the World Bank was because of that event,” Garcia Calao said. “Attend events because you never know what opportunities will arise. I wouldn’t have seen myself working at the World Bank before that.”
After getting an interview, Garcia Calao continued using networking to prepare. He reached out to professionals through LinkedIn, including one connection who eventually became a mentor. Those conversations helped him prepare for his interview, better understand the World Bank and think about what he wanted to do after graduation.
He said his favorite rotation was in the pensions department. Because he previously completed an investment internship, he was familiar with some of the work and felt he could demonstrate the skills he had developed. He worked on two projects and was able to see how his work continued to progress after his rotation ended.
“Sometimes interns can feel like the work they’re doing isn’t important,” Garcia Calao said. “Seeing how something I worked on progressed showed me that the work I did provided value to the team.”
Garcia Calao said his international background became an asset during an internship that brought him into contact with colleagues from around the world. Fluent in Spanish and Italian, he was able to draw on his language skills and experience navigating different cultures.
“Being able to communicate properly with people across the world is important,” Garcia Calao said.
Daniel Garcia Calao, middle row, fourth from right, joins fellow World Bank Treasury interns following their final capstone presentation. Credit: Provided . All Rights Reserved .
Thanks to the Chapel Executive Internship Program, Garcia Calao was able to live right in Washington rather than having to find less expensive housing farther away. Living in Washington also gave Garcia Calao the opportunity to experience the city beyond his internship. He stayed in George Washington University housing, managed his daily commute and explored museums and monuments with fellow interns.
Daniel Garcia Calao participates in the D.C. SCORES tournament while living and working in Washington, D.C., during his summer internship. Credit: Provided . All Rights Reserved .
After he graduates this fall, Garcia Calao will join the pensions department at the World Bank where he completed part of his internship. He said he also hopes to eventually attend graduate school.

articles.title_orig: Star Wars: Galactic Racer launches on Amazon Luna as part of Prime subscription
articles.title_zh: Star Wars: Galactic Racer launches on Amazon Luna as part of Prime subscription
articles.content_orig:
Star Wars: Galactic Racer will be available to play on cloud gaming service Amazon Luna at launch as part of a Prime subscription.
Developed by Fuse Games and published by Secret Mode, players on Amazon Luna will be able to play Galactic Racer's single-player campaign alongside its Arcade and Scenario gameplay modes.
Arcade mode features shorter, time-focused events with specific objectives while the Scenarios mode has different rule-sets and characters to race with.
The game will launch on Luna alongside other platforms including Windows, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X|S.
"We've always believed Luna players deserve to be in the action from day one, and Star Wars: Galactic Racer makes that a reality for the first time," Amazon's Head of Gaming Jeff Gattis tells GamesIndustry.biz.
"Luna players can jump into the single-player campaign the moment it launches without needing to own a console or wait for a lengthy download. If they're a Prime member, they already have it at no additional cost. It's exactly the kind of experience we want to deliver on Luna, and we think players are going to love it."
Amazon Luna launched in the US in 2022 , followed by the UK, Germany, and Canada a year later . The cloud gaming platform became part of Amazon's Prime Video service in the UK and US in July this year.
With additional subscriptions such as Ubisoft+ and linked storefront libraries, Luna has over 100 titles including Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, Hogwarts Legacy, and EA Sports FC 26.
Following Luna's integration into Prime, GamesIndustry.biz spoke with Gattis about the future roadmap for Luna and Amazon Game Studios , and how it intends to target an audience that "don't own dedicated gaming hardware."
"They like to play games, but they're not able to play on a television screen. We think that group's not being served," said Gattis.
"That's an audience that doesn't necessarily want to play AAA competitive shooters, but they do like big IP AAA games. We've done things like Hogwarts Legacy, Indiana Jones, and obviously Tomb Raider in the future. Things that we've found with mass appeal IP that's very approachable, games that aren't incredibly difficult to play, the game mechanics aren't super hard to learn."

articles.title_orig: The GTA VI Rush Is Drying Up New PS5 Pro Stock, and GameStop Now Wants $1,399 for Used Units
articles.title_zh: The GTA VI Rush Is Drying Up New PS5 Pro Stock, and GameStop Now Wants $1,399 for Used Units
articles.content_orig:
A GameStop employee has leaked a substantial PS5 Pro price increase that will go into effect later today , and it's not even for new units .
The following memo was shared internally:
PS5 Pro (preowned) consoles will receive a price change beginning tomorrow, 10/6. Note: the preowned console will have a higher price than the new console - this is intentional. Please ensure all price changes are completed before opening on 10/6.
The memo also said that eligibility for PRP (GameStop's Product Replacement Plan ) will not be available immediately after the price change is completed, but it is planned to be reinstated as soon as possible. Here's the new pricing ($1399 digital, $1499 physical):
Now, you might be wondering why a used console (or any hardware, really) would be priced higher than new units . The reason has everything to do with demand and supply: with Grand Theft Auto VI now a month and a half away from the launch date and the PlayStation 5 Pro set to be the best way to experience the game ( as I pointed out over two years ago ), a lot of casual gamers are just now upgrading to the console generation , making brand new units extremely rare to come by . This has massively inflated the pricing of used units, which are now going for that kind of price on eBay. GameStop is merely playing catch-up.
Of course, that's just one side of the disaster. The PS5 Pro launched in  November 2024 at $699 in the US, which was already a steep ask for a console that shipped without a disc drive, not to mention a big increase over the previous mid-generation refresh (the PS4 Pro shipped in 2016 for $399, the same price as the PS4 launch). It has only become more expensive since .
The first increase arrived on August 21, 2025 , when Sony raised the price of every PS5 model in the US by $50 , taking the Pro to $749.99 . At the time, Sony cited the challenging economic environment, hinting at a direct response to US tariffs. The second, much larger hike took effect worldwide on April 2, 2026. Announced on the PlayStation Blog on March 27 , the price increases raised the standard and Digital Edition PS5 by $100 each and the PS5 Pro by $150 , bringing the more recent console to the current price of $ 899 .
This time, the root cause was component costs . Memory is a key part of any console, PS5 included, and its price surged as manufacturers prioritized the enormous demand coming from AI data centers, leaving supply tight. By the time of the April increase, RAM prices had reportedly risen more than 170% year-over-year, and Ampere Analysis believes Sony had been relying on fixed-price component deals that had since expired, leaving it fully exposed to the market.
This is honestly unprecedented, as consoles used to get cheaper over time, not more expensive . Now, though, a used PS5 Pro Digital at GameStop costs exactly double what a brand-new one did at launch , and with Grand Theft Auto VI arriving on November 19 , it's hard to see demand cooling anytime soon.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX just locked up a NASA record no other U.S. spacecraft can touch
articles.title_zh: SpaceX just locked up a NASA record no other U.S. spacecraft can touch
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX now owns every spot on the list of the five fastest trips a U.S. spacecraft has ever made to the International Space Station, and its newest entry beat the old mark by more than four hours.
Crew Dragon Grace docked to the forward port of the station’s Harmony module at 7:05 p.m. ET on October 1, just 7 hours and 55 minutes after lifting off from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral. NASA confirmed the milestone in a space station blog update , writing that the flight “marked the fastest launch‑to‑docking of a U.S. spacecraft in the history of the International Space Station.”
The previous U.S. record also belonged to Dragon. SpaceX’s uncrewed CRS-31 cargo mission reached the station in a little over 12 hours in November 2024. The fastest crewed trip before last week was Crew-11, which took 14 hours and 43 minutes in August 2025, according to Space.com .
A post that Elon Musk reposted on Monday filled out the rest of the ranking. Behind Crew-13, CRS-31 and Crew-11 sit Axiom’s Ax-2 mission at 15 hours and 35 minutes and NASA’s Crew-4 at 15 hours and 44 minutes. All five flew on Dragon.
SpaceX turned a heralding moment for Starship into its greatest
Crew-13 carried NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. NASA had projected a docking around 8 p.m. ET, as Teslarati reported the day before launch , and Dragon arrived nearly an hour early. Our launch day coverage noted that the flight was lined up to be the quickest Crew Dragon transit yet.
The speed came from timing more than hardware. SpaceX’s Julianna Scheiman said the station “was in an opportune spot in space,” which let Dragon start closing the gap almost immediately after reaching orbit. “This is close to the fastest it could be,” she added. Most Crew Dragon flights still take close to a day, using a series of Draco thruster burns to raise and phase their orbit before arrival.
Dragon’s next job at the station is a departure. NASA said Monday it is targeting 8:05 a.m. ET on Wednesday, October 7, for Crew-12 to undock, setting up a splashdown off the coast of California around 11:34 a.m. on Thursday. Clearing that port makes room for CRS-35, a cargo Dragon carrying the final set of iROSA solar arrays.
Dragon remains NASA’s only operational ride to the station while Boeing’s Starliner stays grounded, and the agency recently added Crew-15, Crew-16 and Crew-17 to SpaceX’s contract in a $946 million modification.

SpaceX reveals plans for one million Starmind AI satellites and calls out operators hiding maneuvers.
SpaceX has put the largest satellite count it has ever published into writing, and it says that plan only works if every other operator in orbit starts sharing what it knows.
In a new Space Safety page highlighted Tuesday morning by Sawyer Merritt on X , SpaceX said it “plans to operate up to 100,000 Starlink satellites and up to 1 million Starmind AI satellites to meet the growing demand for broadband and supercompute.” Starlink has a little over 11,000 satellites in orbit today, so the target alone implies roughly a ninefold expansion of the broadband network.
Starmind is SpaceX’s orbital AI compute constellation. Elon Musk confirmed the Starmind name in June after an xAI trademark filing surfaced, and in August SpaceX said it was working with Nvidia on the compute payload . The FCC accepted the filing for up to one million satellites back in February.
FCC accepts SpaceX filing for 1 million orbital data center plan
SpaceX also released a new render of what a full Starmind constellation could look like. Alongside it, SpaceX VP Michael Nicolls explained why the satellites will not operate on their own. “We need to operate clusters of satellites in tight formation to get enough coherent compute to run AI models efficiently,” Nicolls said . “A cluster will be 10-ish satellites connected with 10 terabits or so of bandwidth between them, and interconnected to the broader constellation.”
That is the most specific detail SpaceX has given on how Starmind will be built. Instead of a million independent servers, the network would work as tightly packed groups of about 10 satellites acting as one compute unit, with Starlink’s laser links carrying results back to Earth.

articles.title_orig: Cornell says ex-US Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates will investigate school’s response to Jane Doe’s rape allegations
articles.title_zh: Cornell says ex-US Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates will investigate school’s response to Jane Doe’s rape allegations
articles.content_orig:
A former Justice Department official will delve into Cornell University’s response to a student’s allegations of gang rape as outrage over the case echoes across the country – from sexual abuse survivors to students on campus and now to the school’s president.
Former US Deputy Attorney General Sally Q. Yates will lead an independent review of how Cornell “prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus,” the university said Tuesday.
That review will include “whether Cornell followed its policies and procedures in responding to” sexual assault allegations brought by a student, known as Jane Doe, against members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024, the university said.
The announcement came after members of Cornell’s Faculty Senate introduced a resolution Monday evening calling for a vote of no confidence against the administration. A vote of no confidence is a formal rebuke of a group’s leadership – and often an attempt to force change or compel resignations.
‘Lack of training, transparency’: Cornell educator addresses crisis on campus
“The faculty have been approached by hundreds of students, alumni, staff who are demanding that we do something,” labor history professor and Faculty Senate member Paul Ortiz told CNN. Some of the students who have approached faculty said they had endured sexual assault, Ortiz said.
“We’re tired of the sexual assaults that happened to our students,” he said. “We’re tired of the administration’s inaction on this issue – and not only our current students, but past students, alumni who have actually given money to this university are fed up.”
Students and community members rallied through streets in Ithaca on Monday evening, chanting “shame” and “resign” after details of the rape allegations came to light in a recently filed civil lawsuit from the former student, known as Jane Doe.
Some groups are also planning to host a seven-hour sit-in on Wednesday “in solidarity with Jane Doe,” according to social media flyers for the event.
The lawsuit Doe filed last month against the university, the Chi Phi fraternity, seven fraternity members and others alleges the school failed to protect her and adequately punish the accused students.
The ensuing fallout has raised questions about how Cornell police handled Jane Doe’s allegations, how much information was shared with the district attorney’s office, the prosecutors’ initial decision not to file charges, and whether the school’s internal investigation and actions went far enough.

articles.title_orig: World Bank warns of AI concentration risks as it lifts East Asia and Pacific growth outlook to 4.5%
articles.title_zh: World Bank warns of AI concentration risks as it lifts East Asia and Pacific growth outlook to 4.5%
articles.content_orig:
The World Bank has raised its growth forecast for the East Asia and Pacific region on the back of artificial intelligence-related exports, while warning that its reliance on the AI boom leaves it vulnerable to a potential global tech spending reversal.
The region includes 23 economies, including China, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand.
The EAP economy is expected to expand 4.5% this year, 0.3 percentage point more than the bank projected in April, according to its latest report released Tuesday. Growth is forecast to ease to 4.4% in 2027 and 4.3% in 2028. Vietnam received the biggest forecast upgrade among major economies of the region, up 1.1 percentage point to 7.4%.
The region's strength, however, is highly dependent on AI-related manufacturing and exports. Trade growth, excluding AI-related goods, has been "weak or negative," the bank said. Those products accounted for more than half of the export growth in most of the region's economies and more than 70% in Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam.
China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam shipped $1.4 trillion of AI-related goods in the 12 months through April, according to the report.
Official data showed that South Korea's exports grew 83.5% in September to a record $120.9 billion , with chips making up half of those shipments. Reflecting the dominance of semiconductors in the country's market, the World Bank highlighted that just two chipmakers — Samsung and SK Hynix — accounted for 43% of the benchmark Kospi index's value as of end-April.
The AI risk is on the spending side. AI-related capital expenditure has reached about 6% of U.S. GDP, similar to the 2000 peak in information-technology investment, and the current cycle "has risen faster than either previous cycle and is still gaining speed," the bank said.
The Bank for International Settlements in its annual economic report in June had warned that the boom's scale and pace bears resemblance to the dot-com frenzy of the 1990s and other "manias."
The financing driving the boom is also less transparent. Of the $2.9 trillion in AI capex planned for 2025-2028, $800 billion is expected to come from private credit, the bank said, where AI-related lending rose to 34% of activity in 2025 from an 18% average over the prior five years. Private credit portfolios have experienced markdowns, outflows and defaults this year.
Private credit markets are "less visible, and have not been tested by a severe downturn," the bank said.
That said, the AI boom supported by abundant liquidity could slow due to the latest tightening of financial conditions as major central banks raise rates for the first time since 2023, according to the report. The U.S. Federal Reserve raised rates last month , its first increase in more than three years, and signaled one more to hike this year.
A correction may not necessarily mean a bust for the AI supercycle, but that investment "had run ahead of realized demand," the organization said.
A slowdown by 1 percentage point in U.S. growth cuts other emerging-market growth by an estimated 0.6 percentage point, with the hit to investment about twice as large, the bank said. "A slowdown concentrated in AI would be material for East Asia because of the region's prominence in the AI supply chain."
Bank funding is the broadest exposure. Foreign-currency-denominated liabilities of banks appeared significant in some countries — 29.2% of GDP in Malaysia, 20.7% in the Philippines.
Taiwan's statistics bureau recently raised its 2026 growth forecast to 11% from 9.6% on AI demand, while warning in June that "if the high-tech sector faces headwinds, the negative impact on the local economy could be bigger than expected."

Many white dwarfs accrete the debris of disrupted planetary bodies, detected in the form of metal enrichment in their atmospheres, dusty or gaseous circumstellar discs, and photometric transits from debris. The composition of accreted debris has been shown to be diverse yet overall closely resembles Solar System bodies. Here we report the discovery of a white dwarf accreting material that is unlike any Solar System object. The atmosphere of HS 0209+0832 is strongly enriched in trans-iron elements including zinc, copper and niobium but depleted in the canonical rock-forming elements silicon and iron. The composition of the accreted object is consistent with a candidate second-generation planet, formed from the stellar material ejected during the giant phase. The key abundance signature that differentiates it from a first-generation planet is the high enrichment of s-process elements. Photospheric helium and the absence of terrestrial rock-forming elements implies that the white dwarf is accreting from the escaped atmosphere of a photo-evaporating giant planet candidate. This is further supported by the detection of a sinusoidal photometric period of 4.399 ± 0.026 days at an amplitude of 0.120% ± 0.018%, which we attribute to thermal emission phase variability from a planetary day–night cycle or a transiting cometary tail of an evaporating gas giant. The discovery of this second-generation planet that is chemically distinct from first-generation material demonstrates that close-in planets around white dwarfs can form after the main sequence.
HS 0209+0832 is a hot, young white dwarf with an effective temperature of T eff ≈ 35,000 K, a cooling age of t cool ≈ 5 Myr and a hydrogen-dominated atmosphere with an ~1% trace of helium 1 . Such a mixed composition is unusual for a white dwarf of this temperature because helium should sink out of the atmosphere within months 2 , 3 . A far-ultraviolet (FUV) spectrum obtained in 1999 with the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) onboard the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) revealed the presence of carbon, aluminium, silicon, calcium, titanium, nickel and zinc in the atmosphere 4 , as well as ~100 lines that could not be identified. Whereas the presence of helium and metals indicates ongoing accretion, the nature of that external source remained unexplained 4 .
In the 25 years since that study was published, the origin of photospheric metals detected in many other white dwarfs has been unambiguously confirmed as planetary debris 5 , 6 . This motivated a reanalysis of the observations of HS 0209+0832 obtained with HST/STIS, the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) and the Ultraviolet and Visual Echelle Spectrograph (UVES) mounted on the Very Large Telescope (VLT), along with the broad-band photometry from Pan-STARRS and the Gaia parallax ( Methods ). In a first step, we determined T eff = 35,800 ± 500 K, a surface gravity of log g = 7.90 ± 0.02 and a helium abundance of log(He/H) = −1.90 ± 0.20 (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Extended Data Table 1 ). With these parameters fixed, we computed extensive grids of synthetic white dwarf spectra 7 using detailed lists of metal transitions in the ultraviolet (Extended Data Table 2 ). We matched most of the previously unidentified lines to transitions of copper and niobium, with the latter identified using five Nb III lines and 57 Nb IV lines (Fig. 1 ). We carefully examined archival FUSE 8 spectra of 33 known metal-enriched white dwarfs with temperatures 20,000 K < T eff < 77,000 K and confirm non-detections for niobium within that sample.
The FUSE and HST spectra (both black) of HS 0209+0832 contain many lines of C, Al, Si, Ca, Ti, Ni, Cu, Zn and Nb as well as strong hydrogen and helium lines. The unusual structure of the He II line is not well reproduced by the model, which could be caused by additional absorption from circumstellar gas. We show the model fit used to obtain metal abundances in red.
We measured the photospheric abundances ( Methods ) for nine metals and calculated upper limits on 15 metals (Extended Data Table 3 ). We excluded any lines originating from the interstellar medium in our fit (Extended Data Table 4 ). At the temperature of HS 0209+0832, radiative levitation can support certain elements against gravitational diffusion. We investigated this effect for all detected elements, as well as for N, P and S for which we determined upper limits ( Methods ). We selected these volatiles because they are commonly detected in hot white dwarfs 8 , 9 ; thus, it is unusual they are not observed in HS 0209+0832. We find that, for the measured abundances, radiative levitation is negligible for Ca, S, Ti, Ni, Cu, Zn and Nb. Assuming a steady state between accretion into and diffusion out of the white dwarf atmosphere, we computed the diffusion fluxes for each element. We adopt these mass fluxes as being representative of the material accreting onto HS 0209+0832, as they correct the photospheric abundances for the differential sinking timescales of individual metals (Extended Data Table 3 ). By contrast, the abundances of C, N, Al, Si and P are subject to radiative support. These elements must still have an external origin 10 , 11 , but our analysis cannot determine their mass fractions within the accreting material.
We compare the abundances of the parent body accreting onto HS 0209+0832 to the entire sample of white dwarfs accreting rocky material 12 and to Solar System meteorites 13 , but find no compositional matches (Fig. 2 ). Whereas silicon and iron are two major components of planetary bodies in the inner Solar System, with a combined mass fraction of ~48% in the bulk Earth 14 , we detect only traces of silicon in the atmosphere of HS 0209+0832, compatible with the support provided by radiative levitation, and no iron. By contrast, the material accreting onto HS 0209+0832 is rich in nickel, which shares many geochemical properties with iron, and we measure a nickel-to-iron ratio of Ni/Fe > 2.09, compared with ~0.05 within CI chondrites 15 and the bulk Earth 14 . We find that the trans-iron elements are strongly enhanced relative to calcium compared with solar abundances, particularly niobium, which is over three orders of magnitude more abundant than in the Sun.
We show the number abundances of the metals (Z) in the material accreting onto HS 0209+0832 (red stars) with respect to calcium, normalized to bulk Earth (BE) 74 (solid black line) for all detected metals and metals with strict upper limits. The error bars represent 1 σ uncertainties, and the arrows represent upper limits. The dashed red lines represent the predicted abundance from radiative levitation alone. For comparison, we include the solar abundance pattern 75 (dashed black line), comet Halley 76 (black points) and the abundances of several white dwarfs accreting bulk Earth-like 5 , core-rich 77 , mantle-rich 78 and icy 16 material (green, blue, brown and purple points, respectively).
Most enriched white dwarfs are depleted in volatile elements such as C, N and S, but a minority are volatile enriched, which can be due to accreting either icy bodies 16 or the atmosphere of a giant planet 17 . The only volatile detected in HS 0209+0832 is carbon (Extended Data Fig. 2 ), with a high photospheric abundance that is compatible with fiducial predictions from radiative levitation. However, there are both theoretical and empirical reasons to believe that our fiducial radiative levitation predictions overestimate the importance of this effect. You may have watched the moon block out the sun during a solar eclipse , but have you ever seen it do that to a planet? Early Tuesday (Oct. 6) morning, skywatchers across much of eastern North America will have an opportunity to watch a crescent moon pass directly in front of Jupiter. The rare alignment won't happen again for 11 years.
During the event, known as a lunar occultation, Jupiter will disappear behind the moon for up to about an hour before suddenly reappearing. The occultation will be visible before dawn from much of the eastern and central U.S., Canada and the Caribbean, while parts of Africa will experience the event during daylight, according to In-The-Sky.org .
The moon will be a beautiful waning crescent, just 20% illuminated, and Jupiter will shine brightly alongside it. The pair will rise together in the east early Tuesday morning and gradually appear to move closer as the moon travels eastward against the background stars.
When the occultation begins, Jupiter will remain hidden behind the moon for roughly an hour. No telescope will be needed to watch Jupiter disappear and reappear. However, a pair of binoculars or a small telescope will make the event much more dramatic.
Through a telescope, Jupiter will look like a tiny disc rather than a point of light and will take about a minute to disappear completely behind the moon. An easy way to photograph the event is to use a smart telescope to image the moon. (Here's everything you need to know about lunar photography ).
Below are the times when Jupiter will disappear and reappear in 10 major cities Tuesday morning, according to the International Occultation Timing Association .
Outside the occultation path, Jupiter won't disappear at all. Instead, it will appear to be skimmed by the crescent moon — still a potentially spectacular sight that could produce some amazing photos. From across much of the world, the crescent moon and Jupiter will appear exceptionally close together.

Unpasteurized milk and milk products pose serious infection risks to pregnant people, infants, and children, and should be banned nationwide, according to an AAP policy statement published in Pediatrics .
Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) may represent a safe treatment approach for managing positional plagiocephaly in infants, according to Kimberly Wolf, DO, and colleagues.
“A flat head is a common reason parents bring their infants to the pediatrician in the first few months of life — yet until now, families have had strikingly few choices for treatment,” Wolf said in a news release .
Teddy bears fitted with medical devices such as gastrostomy tubes, tracheostomies, and pacemakers may help normalize these devices and reduce anxiety in children who need them, according to a project described at the AAP meeting.

Astronomers have discovered a rare second-generation planet orbiting the ashes of the dead star from which it was born, a smoldering white dwarf.
Though scientists have long suspected that reborn planets could orbit more massive stellar remnants called neutron stars , this is the first time astronomers have discovered a second-generation planet orbiting a white dwarf . The discovery matters for our understanding of the future of the solar system , since a the sun will leave behind a white dwarf stellar remnant when it dies in about 6 billion years.
The astronomers behind this discovery say it was a total surprise. "Second-generation planets are worlds that form out of the material a star casts off as it dies. They're incredibly rare, and finding one around a white dwarf was completely unexpected," team member Jamie Williams of the University of Warwick said in a statement sent to Space.com. "It's a bit like finding a planet that has risen from the ashes of the very star it once orbited."
White dwarfs are created when stars around the size of the sun exhaust the hydrogen in their cores needed to fuel nuclear fusion and create helium. The end of this nuclear process also ends the outward pressure that stops stars from collapsing under the inward push of their own gravity. As the cores of these dead stars collapse, the outer layers where nuclear fusion is still occurring swell out, beginning a short-lived red giant phase. When our sun undergoes this process, it will puff out to around the orbit of Mars, swallowing the inner planets, including Earth.
These puffed-out outer layers continue to expand until they form a disk of material far out from the star called a protoplanetary disk, leaving behind a cosmic ember in the form of a smoldering white dwarf. Some white dwarfs can strip material from the planets that remain orbiting around them, and this process can be investigated by the detection of rock-forming elements like silicon and iron.
The white dwarf at the heart of this research is HS 0209+0832, located around 790 light-years from Earth. The atmosphere of this stellar remnant contains unusually high levels zinc, copper, and, most notably, niobium, with concentrations around 1,000 times greater than the sun . That told this team something remarkable about the planet that this white dwarf has been snacking on.
"This pattern of elements is a telltale sign of the 's-process,' a nuclear reaction that builds heavy elements inside dying stars during their bloated red giant phase," said Nicholas Stone, of the Department of Astronomy at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "It's a chemical signature no ordinary, 'first-generation' planet should carry, which told us that this new planet was something different."
The team thinks that this unique chemical signature indicates this white dwarf is stealing material from a planet that formed in the protoplanetary disk of material shed by the dying star during its red giant phase.
"Forming the protoplanetary disc in this situation is not easy and helps explain why these planets are so rare. A single, isolated star dies and sheds mass in a roughly symmetrical way," Williams added. "To form a disc of material necessary to birth a planet, HS 0209+0832 likely required a companion star that pulled the ejected material back into orbit, rather than letting it escape."
The team further investigated this second-generation planet using NASA's exoplanet hunting spacecraft TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite), which searches for planets beyond the solar system by observing the dips in light they cause as they cross the face of their parent stars.
The dip in light from HS 0209+0832 indicated this Phoenix world has an orbit of around 4.4 Earth days and is a Jupiter-sized gas giant. The stellar radiation the planet experiences due to its proximity to its white dwarf will eventually boil its atmosphere away. And as that radiation strikes the white dwarf it gives rise to the unique chemical signature seen by the team.
That chemical signature might be a way forward that could help astronomers hunt for more of these 'rebirth' planets.
"What's remarkable about the planet around HS 0209+0832 is that this isn't a planet from somewhere else, or a survivor from the system's birth; it looks like it was built from the very material its own star cast off as it died. In a sense, this system has given birth to a new world using the foundations of the old one," team member Boris Gänsicke of the University of Warwick said.
"Finding this one example raises the question of how many more might be out there and might our own solar system host a second-generation planet formed from the ashes of our sun."
The team's research was published on Monday (Oct. 5) in Nature Astronomy ,
